title: How Anti-Dieting Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the anti-dieting movement, a response to diet culture that rejects dieting, weight-loss goals, and fat shaming, and promotes intuitive eating. They walk through the ten principles of intuitive eating (developed by registered dietitians Evelyn Tribole and Elyse Resch), discuss the body's starvation response and "set point" theory, the claimed link between dieting and weight regain, the debate over whether an obesity epidemic exists (citing a 2006 Campos law professor survey on BMI and mortality), the role of nutrition, and the body-positivity backlash around Ashley Graham. The episode opens with a book plug for Stuff You Should Know: An Incomplete Compendium of Mostly Interesting Things, and closes with a listener mail about the 1843 Change Water massacres in Jenny's family history.

entities.name: Stuff You Should Know: An Incomplete Compendium of Mostly Interesting Things

segments.title: Book plug and opening
segments.summary: Hosts promote their upcoming book Stuff You Should Know: An Incomplete Compendium of Mostly Interesting Things, then introduce the episode on the anti-dieting movement prompted by listener suggestions.

segments.title: What the anti-diet movement is
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck define the anti-dieting movement as a response to diet culture that rejects dieting, weight-loss focus, and fat shaming, and says diets don't work, and that food should be enjoyed and bodies accepted. They note intuitive eating is its central focus but only part of the larger movement, and that intuitive eating is not a diet.

segments.title: Intuitive eating origins and childhood hunger cues
segments.summary: Intuitive eating was developed in the 1990s by registered dietitians Evelyn Tribole and Elyse Resch. The hosts describe the argument that babies naturally eat when hungry and stop when full, and that adults lose these cues due to diet culture.

segments.title: Ten principles of intuitive eating
segments.summary: The hosts walk through the principles: rejecting the diet mentality, honoring hunger, making peace with food, challenging the food police, respecting fullness (including the Japanese hara hachi bu practice), satisfaction, honoring feelings without food, respecting your body, exercise for mood rather than weight loss, and gentle nutrition.

segments.title: Set point theory, starvation response and diet-induced obesity
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the claim that diets trigger a biological starvation response, with hunger and binge eating, and that the body may raise its fat set point, leading to regain and even higher weight, a phenomenon called diet-induced obesity. They also cover calorie-restrictive diets that are said to work short-term and the unhealthy diets such as the cabbage soup, grapefruit, Sleeping Beauty and feeding tube diets, and mention Weight Watchers and Jenny Craig.

segments.title: Obesity epidemic debate and BMI mortality study
segments.summary: Anti-diet proponents argue there is no public health crisis, citing average weight gains of six to eleven pounds and a 2006 survey by law professor Campos of medical literature finding that overweight and lower obesity ranges carry little added mortality risk. The hosts say this is not a complete answer and that the claim is somewhat glib.

segments.title: Nutrition, healthy at every size, and body positivity backlash
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the role of nutrition, noting dietitians support anti-dieting and Healthy at Every Size (founded by Linda Bacon in 2010) but emphasize whole foods. They describe backlash against Ashley Graham after she lost weight, the division in the movement, and the difficulty of relearning hunger signals, referencing a 2017 study of retired female athletes and former NFL players.

segments.title: Sign-off and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode, then read a listener email from Jenny about her family's ancestors killed in the 1843 Cahnge Water massacres by axe murderers, with two boys surviving.
